screens.title: Keyboard Input and String Handling
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we study two complementary pieces of the Jack OS: the Keyboard module, which reads user keystrokes, and the String module, which stores and manipulates text. You will learn how non‑blocking checks differ from blocking reads, why readChar waits for a release, and how strings are implemented with length, maxLength and a character array allocated from the heap. These pieces matter because interactive programs — asking a user for a name, parsing numbers, or building typed input — depend on reliable input handling and predictable memory for text. A concrete example you will build is a short program that prompts for a name, greets the user, reads two integers, and prints their sum. Along the way you’ll see how to avoid a common pitfall: without release detection a single physical key press can appear as many characters. As you move through the screens, I’ll show polling code, string constructors that call Memory. alloc, and the integer-to-string and string-to-integer conversions. Think about why Jack leaves memory management manual: it keeps the runtime simple and forces you to reason about when to allocate and free objects. By the end, you’ll be able to implement the Keyboard and String modules and compose them to write small interactive programs. What interactive prompt will you try first?

screens.title: Keyboard Module Overview
screens.narratorSegment: The Keyboard module offers a small set of functions that let programs observe and read keyboard input. The central primitive is keyPressed, which is a non‑blocking query that returns the ASCII code of a pressed key or zero when no key is pressed. Non‑blocking checks are useful when a program must continue doing work if no input exists, for example updating a screen or checking timers without stalling. In contrast, blocking functions like readChar wait until input appears. Blocking reads are appropriate when the next action truly depends on the user, such as reading a confirmation or a typed character for a prompt. A useful mental model is a telegraph operator: keyPressed is a quick peek at the line to see if a dot arrived; readChar is the operator sitting patiently until a full signal arrives. A common misconception is thinking keyPressed and readChar are interchangeable; they are not — one returns immediately while the other suspends execution. As a concrete example, a game loop might use keyPressed to poll controls so the simulation continues smoothly, whereas a login prompt should call readLine or readInt to wait for the user's response. Takeaway: choose non‑blocking checks for responsive loops, and blocking reads when the program must stop and wait for input.

keyIdea.title: Non‑blocking versus blocking
keyIdea.text: Use keyPressed when you must keep running; use readChar/readLine/readInt when the program must wait for user input.

content.html:
Core Concept
Definition
What the Keyboard module offers
A compact API to check and read keystrokes: keyPressed, readChar, readLine, readInt.
keyPressed(): non-blocking — returns ASCII or 0 immediately.
readChar(): blocking — waits for press and release to return a single char.
readLine(message): prompt and return a line ending with Enter.
readInt(message): prompt and parse an integer from typed text.
Example
A game loop polls keyPressed to move characters without stopping the simulation.
Common mistake
Using readChar in a tight loop when you needed non‑blocking checks causes the program to freeze until a key is pressed.
Quick reference: behavior and use
  • keyPressed returns 0 when idle. Use it to poll for input without pausing your program.
  • readChar waits for a press and a release to ensure one character per physical press.
  • readLine combines prompts and collection of a sequence of characters until Enter.
  • readInt reads characters, parses an integer, and returns its numeric value.
Key Takeaway

Match your read method to whether the program must wait. Polling keeps things running; blocking reads are for direct interaction.

screens.title: Implementing readChar with Polling
screens.narratorSegment: The readChar implementation shown in the chapter uses a two-phase polling approach: wait for a key press, read the value, then wait for the key to be released. This pattern guarantees that a physical press produces one character regardless of how long the key is held. Concretely, the code loops until keyPressed returns a non‑zero value; it stores that value; then it loops until keyPressed becomes zero, indicating release. Finally it returns the stored character. This is crucial on the Hack platform because the keyboard hardware presents the key code continuously while the key remains depressed. A subtle point is why we store the character immediately after detecting the press rather than reading it only once the release occurs. If you waited until release you might miss short presses that happen between polls. The concrete example in the chapter demonstrates the exact code. A common misconception is that a single loop checking keyPressed once is sufficient — it's not, because you must also wait for release. Takeaway: the two loops create a single atomic press event in software. Try mentally stepping through a press-and-hold and verify that only one character would be returned.

If you waited until release you might miss short presses that happen between polls. The concrete example in the chapter demonstrates the exact code. keyIdea.title: Two‑phase polling
keyIdea.text: Wait for a press, capture the character, then wait for release so each physical press yields one character.

content.html:
Process Flow
readChar — Poll until press and release
Annotated code walkthrough. The code blocks below show the polling pattern described in the chapter. Note the explicit storage of c and the second loop waiting for release.
function char readChar() {
  var char c;
  // Wait for a key press
  while (Keyboard.keyPressed() = 0) {}
  let c = Keyboard.keyPressed();
  // Wait for key release
  while (~(Keyboard.keyPressed() = 0)) {}
  return c;
}
Why store immediately
Storing on press avoids missing fast presses that could occur between poll cycles.
Release detection
Waiting for release prevents repeated returns while a key is held down.
Step-by-step example
  1. Loop until keyPressed() != 0 — that is, detect the press.
  2. Read and store the ASCII code into local variable c.
  3. Loop until keyPressed() == 0 — detect the release.
  4. Return c so the caller receives one character per press.
Common Mistake
If you skip release detection, holding a key outputs the same character repeatedly.
Key Takeaway

The press-then-release polling pattern creates atomic key events on simple hardware.

screens.title: readLine and readInt: Prompts and Parsing
screens.narratorSegment: The chapter describes two higher‑level helpers that combine key reads and string operations. readLine displays a prompt message, then collects characters until the user presses Enter, returning the assembled string. readInt displays a prompt and collects characters that form an integer, then converts that text into a numeric value. Together they simplify user interaction: you call the helper, the function performs the low‑level reads and parsing, and your program receives a usable string or integer. A concrete example: to ask for a user's name you call readLine("Name: "), the routine will echo typed characters into a String object and stop when Enter is detected, returning the String. To request a number, call readInt("Number: "); the routine reads digits, handles a leading minus if present, and converts the text into an integer before returning. A common pitfall is trusting the input will always be valid; readInt assumes digits are provided or performs simple parsing — your program should consider input validation. Takeaway: prefer these helpers when you need a complete user response instead of manual low‑level reads. readLine and readInt: Prompts and Parsing means readline collects characters into a dynamic string until enter; readint reads characters and parses them into an integer value.. In practical terms, collecting a line of text and parsing numeric input. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: readLine collects characters into a dynamic string until Enter; readInt reads characters and parses them into an integer value.

content.html:
Definition
readLine and readInt
How readLine works (process)
  1. Display the prompt message to the output.
  2. Create a new String object with a maxLength.
  3. Call readChar repeatedly to append characters until Enter is detected.
  4. Return the constructed String to the caller.
Example
Call readLine("Name: ") and expect a String containing the user's typed name after Enter.
How readInt works (process)
  1. Display the prompt message.
  2. Read characters forming an integer, allowing an optional leading minus sign.
  3. Append digits into a String and then convert with intValue, or parse on the fly.
  4. Return the integer numeric value to the caller.
Practical note
Implementations often reuse String operations for collection and then call intValue to parse the result.
Check Your Understanding
Why prefer readInt to manual parsing when requesting a number?
Misconception
Assuming readLine always trims input; it returns exactly the collected characters up to Enter.
Key Takeaway

Use readLine/readInt for full user responses; implement validation if input may be malformed.

screens.title: String Module Structure
screens.narratorSegment: In Jack, a string is represented as an object with a small fixed layout: a length field for the current number of characters, a maxLength that records the allocated capacity, and a charArray pointer that references the dynamically allocated character buffer. The buffer itself is allocated using Memory. alloc. Because the string object contains references and a pointer to additional heap storage, it must be constructed at runtime using String. new and later disposed if no longer needed. This differs from static arrays because each string can have a different maxLength and can be resized by creating a larger buffer and copying content if desired. A concrete example: calling String. new(64) would allocate space for the String object and call Memory. alloc(64) to reserve a charArray of 64 characters. The length starts at zero. appendChar increments length and writes into the next slot; eraseLastChar decrements length. A common misconception is assuming strings are fixed or implicitly garbage collected; in Jack they are explicit objects managed by the programmer. Takeaway: think of a string as a small header plus a separately allocated character buffer managed through Memory. alloc and explicit lifecycle calls.

keyIdea.title: String = header + buffer
keyIdea.text: Strings are objects holding length, maxLength, and a pointer to a Memory.alloc‑ed charArray; they must be created and disposed explicitly.

content.html:
Definition
String module structure
Fields of a String object
  • length — current number of stored characters.
  • maxLength — allocated capacity of the charArray.
  • charArray — pointer to a block allocated by Memory.alloc(maxLength).
Example
String.new(32) allocates a new object and calls Memory.alloc(32) for the character storage.
Memory implications
Because the charArray is a separate allocation, strings incur two allocations: one for the object header and one for the buffer. This is why explicit allocation and deallocation are required in the Jack OS.
Common Pitfall
Forgetting to set maxLength properly can lead to buffer overflows when appending characters.
Key Takeaway

Treat strings as objects with explicit allocation and predictable layout: length, capacity, and a char array pointer.

screens.title: String Operations: Append, Index, Erase
screens.narratorSegment: The String module exposes operations that manipulate the header and the charArray. appendChar checks that the current length is less than maxLength, writes the new character into charArray[length], and increments length. charAt returns charArray[i] after bounds checking. setCharAt writes to the given index if within bounds. eraseLastChar decrements length and may optionally clear the slot. These operations are simple but the implementation must carefully manage length and ensure not to write past maxLength. A concrete example: consider appending three characters to a newly created string new(4). After each append length increases 0→1→2→3 and the characters occupy indices 0,1,2. If you try to append a fifth character you should either return an error or ignore the append, depending on your design. A common misconception is assuming that appendChar will automatically grow the buffer; in Jack, buffer growth requires explicit allocation and copying. Takeaway: test edge cases: empty strings, full buffers, and invalid indices for charAt and setCharAt so your code fails predictably rather than corrupting memory. String Operations: Append, Index, Erase means append and set operations must enforce capacity checks; erase and indexing must respect length to avoid memory corruption.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Process Flow
String operations
Append and index behavior
appendChar: if (length < maxLength) write charArray[length] = c; length++.
charAt(i): if (0 ≤ i && i < length) return charArray[i]; otherwise handle error.
Example
String.new(4); append 'a','b','c' results in length 3 and indices 0..2 filled.
Edge case
Appending when length == maxLength should be rejected or cause a controlled failure.
Erase and set operations
eraseLastChar: if length > 0 then length--. Optionally clear charArray[length] = 0 for safety. setCharAt(i,c): write only if 0 ≤ i < length or you may expand to i < maxLength depending on your design.
Misconception
Assuming setCharAt can increase length automatically. In Jack, changing length should be explicit to avoid silent buffer changes.
Key Takeaway

Implement bounds checks for every operation; do not rely on implicit buffer growth.

screens.title: Memory Allocation for Strings
screens.narratorSegment: The chapter explains that strings are objects and their character buffers are allocated dynamically via the Memory module. When String. new(maxLength) is called, the implementation typically calls Memory. alloc(maxLength) to reserve a contiguous block of memory for the characters and stores the returned base address in charArray. The string object itself is also allocated so the runtime holds both the header and the buffer pointer. This two‑allocation pattern is straightforward but has important implications: memory must be managed explicitly and fragmentation is possible if many different sizes are allocated and freed. As a concrete example, creating many small temporary strings without deallocating them will consume heap space and eventually fail. A common misconception is expecting automatic deallocation; Jack OS provides no garbage collector, so Memory. deAlloc or a manual convention must be used in the implementations you write. Takeaway: design your string usage with allocation costs in mind — reuse buffers when possible and free them when done. The next screen shows a compact pseudo‑code sketch for String. new and dispose to clarify the pattern. Memory Allocation for Strings means string.new allocates an object plus a chararray via memory.alloc; manual deallocation is required to avoid leaks.. In practical terms, how memory.alloc is used to create the chararray buffer. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Two allocations per string
keyIdea.text: String.new allocates an object plus a charArray via Memory.alloc; manual deallocation is required to avoid leaks.

content.html:
Architecture
Memory allocation pattern
Allocation sketch
// pseudo-code sketch
function String new(maxLength) {
  var String s;
  let s = Memory.alloc(OBJECT_SIZE);
  let s.length = 0;
  let s.maxLength = maxLength;
  let s.charArray = Memory.alloc(maxLength);
  return s;
}

function void disposeString(String s) {
  Memory.deAlloc(s.charArray);
  Memory.deAlloc(s);
}
This shows the two allocations: one for the object header and one for the character buffer returned by Memory.alloc.
Practical implications
  • Every new string consumes heap space twice: header and buffer.
  • Manual deallocation is mandatory to avoid memory leaks.
  • Reusing buffers or reserving a larger maxLength can improve performance.
Why it matters

Allocations are explicit in Jack; mindful allocation and deallocation are essential to robust programs.

screens.title: Integer-to-String and String-to-Integer
screens.narratorSegment: The String module includes two complementary conversions. setInt converts an integer into its textual representation: it handles negative numbers by recording the sign, extracts digits by repeatedly dividing the absolute value by ten, collects digits in reverse order, and then reverses them into the charArray. intValue parses a numeric string into an integer by scanning digits, accumulating the value by multiplying the running total by ten and adding the next digit, and handling an optional leading minus sign. keyIdea.text: setInt uses repeated division and reverse collection; intValue uses digit accumulation with multiplication by ten.

content.html:
Definition
Integer ↔ String conversions
setInt (integer to string)
  1. Handle sign: if negative, remember to prepend '-'.
  2. For positive absolute value, repeat: digit = value % 10; push digit as character; value = value / 10.
  3. Reverse collected digits to produce correct order and write into charArray.
Example: setInt(-123) builds characters '1','2','3' in reverse, then produces "-123" after reversal.
intValue (string to integer)
  1. Check for a leading minus to set sign.
  2. Initialize total = 0 and for each digit character do total = total * 10 + (digitValue).
  3. Return sign * total at the end.
Example: parsing "456" yields 4 then 45 then 456 by accumulation.
Key Takeaway

setInt and intValue are mirror algorithms: one extracts digits via division, the other accumulates via multiplication by ten.

screens.title: Polling vs Event-driven Input
screens.narratorSegment: The chapter focuses on polling because the Hack platform provides a memory-mapped keyboard register and no kernel event queue. Polling repeatedly checks that register to detect key presses. This contrasts with event-driven input, where hardware or an interrupt system notifies the OS when a key event happens, and the OS queues an event for programs. Polling is simple and predictable: code checks and acts. Event-driven systems can be more efficient because the C P U can sleep until an interrupt wakes it, avoiding busy loops. A concrete contrast: keyPressed in Jack is a quick non‑blocking check reading a register; in an event-driven OS you might register a callback or read from an input buffer filled by interrupt handlers. Misconception: polling always wastes C P U — with well-placed pauses or cooperative scheduling, polling can be acceptable in small systems. Takeaway: Jack's polling model is chosen for simplicity and educational clarity; understand it so you can reason about C P U usage, responsiveness, and how release detection must be implemented in polling systems to avoid repeated characters. Comparison
Polling versus event-driven input
Polling (Jack example)
  • Program checks keyPressed repeatedly.
  • Simple implementation, easy to reason about.
  • Requires release detection to avoid repeated characters.
Event-driven

  • Generally avoids busy waiting but requires more runtime infrastructure.
Reflection
Jack’s polling model is intentionally simple for instructional purposes. Consider what changes are needed if the platform provided an interrupt-driven keyboard: you would move release detection into the interrupt handler and publish single events to the OS input queue.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Debugging Strategies
screens.narratorSegment: When implementing the Keyboard and String modules, a few patterns produce recurring bugs. First, missing release detection in readChar causes repeated characters when a key is held. To debug this, log the raw keyPressed values or write a small test program that prints a single marker per readChar call while you press and hold a key. Second, off‑by‑one errors in appendChar or setCharAt can overwrite memory; always assert bounds before writing and test with edge lengths such as zero, one, and full capacity. Third, failing to allocate enough maxLength for setInt output can truncate results. A practical debugging strategy: build small unit tests for each operation. For strings, test new(maxLength), appendChar until full, call eraseLastChar repeatedly, and verify length changes as expected. For keyboard, test keyPressed returns zero when idle and that readChar returns one character per press. If you see crashes, check that every Memory. alloc has a matching Memory. deAlloc if your environment requires it. A misconception is assuming printing the whole string always verifies correctness — also test internal length and charAt values. Takeaway: write unit checks for edge cases and run the simple prompt program repeatedly while observing behavior to locate timing and allocation bugs.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we study two complementary pieces of the Jack OS: the Keyboard module, which reads user keystrokes, and the String module, which stores and manipulates text. You will learn how non‑blocking checks differ from blocking reads, why readChar waits for a release, and how strings are implemented with length, maxLength and a character array allocated from the heap. These pieces matter because interactive programs — asking a user for a name, parsing numbers, or building typed input — depend on reliable input handling and predictable memory for text. A concrete example you will build is a short program that prompts for a name, greets the user, reads two integers, and prints their sum. Along the way you’ll see how to avoid a common pitfall: without release detection a single physical key press can appear as many characters. As you move through the screens, I’ll show polling code, string constructors that call Memory. alloc, and the integer-to-string and string-to-integer conversions. Think about why Jack leaves memory management manual: it keeps the runtime simple and forces you to reason about when to allocate and free objects. By the end, you’ll be able to implement the Keyboard and String modules and compose them to write small interactive programs. What interactive prompt will you try first?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to implement the Keyboard module, distinguishing non‑blocking checks from blocking reads so your programs respond correctly to user input. For example, you will know when to use a quick check that returns zero if nothing is pressed versus waiting for a full key press and release. You will also understand how to implement readChar so it detects a press and then waits for release, preventing single physical presses from producing repeated characters. Next, you will learn how to design the String module: allocate a character array with a maxLength, maintain a current length, and implement common operations such as appendChar, eraseLastChar, and conversions to and from integers. Finally, you will practice composing keyboard reads and string operations to build simple interactive programs. Each objective is tied to a verified competency milestone so you can confirm you implemented the module functions and wrote a working prompt-and-parse program.

This second objectives screen ties each goal to a concrete implementation and a small verification check. For the Keyboard module you will implement keyPressed as a non‑blocking read of the memory-mapped keyboard register and then test it by printing its value when a key is present. For readChar you will implement a polling loop that waits for a key press, reads the character, then waits for release. To verify it, press and hold a key and confirm only one character appears. For strings you will implement a constructor that calls Memory. alloc to reserve a charArray and a length field, then test appendChar and eraseLastChar to confirm length updates correctly. Finally, for interactive composition you will write a small program that asks for a name, greets the user, then requests two integers and prints their sum. These concrete checks map directly to the verified milestones and give you repeatable tests for correctness.

The Keyboard module offers a small set of functions that let programs observe and read keyboard input. The central primitive is keyPressed, which is a non‑blocking query that returns the ASCII code of a pressed key or zero when no key is pressed. Non‑blocking checks are useful when a program must continue doing work if no input exists, for example updating a screen or checking timers without stalling. In contrast, blocking functions like readChar wait until input appears. Blocking reads are appropriate when the next action truly depends on the user, such as reading a confirmation or a typed character for a prompt. A useful mental model is a telegraph operator: keyPressed is a quick peek at the line to see if a dot arrived; readChar is the operator sitting patiently until a full signal arrives. A common misconception is thinking keyPressed and readChar are interchangeable; they are not — one returns immediately while the other suspends execution. As a concrete example, a game loop might use keyPressed to poll controls so the simulation continues smoothly, whereas a login prompt should call readLine or readInt to wait for the user's response. Takeaway: choose non‑blocking checks for responsive loops, and blocking reads when the program must stop and wait for input.

The readChar implementation shown in the chapter uses a two-phase polling approach: wait for a key press, read the value, then wait for the key to be released. This pattern guarantees that a physical press produces one character regardless of how long the key is held. Concretely, the code loops until keyPressed returns a non‑zero value; it stores that value; then it loops until keyPressed becomes zero, indicating release. Finally it returns the stored character. This is crucial on the Hack platform because the keyboard hardware presents the key code continuously while the key remains depressed. A subtle point is why we store the character immediately after detecting the press rather than reading it only once the release occurs. If you waited until release you might miss short presses that happen between polls. The concrete example in the chapter demonstrates the exact code. A common misconception is that a single loop checking keyPressed once is sufficient — it's not, because you must also wait for release. Takeaway: the two loops create a single atomic press event in software. Try mentally stepping through a press-and-hold and verify that only one character would be returned.

The chapter describes two higher‑level helpers that combine key reads and string operations. readLine displays a prompt message, then collects characters until the user presses Enter, returning the assembled string. readInt displays a prompt and collects characters that form an integer, then converts that text into a numeric value. Together they simplify user interaction: you call the helper, the function performs the low‑level reads and parsing, and your program receives a usable string or integer. A concrete example: to ask for a user's name you call readLine("Name: "), the routine will echo typed characters into a String object and stop when Enter is detected, returning the String. To request a number, call readInt("Number: "); the routine reads digits, handles a leading minus if present, and converts the text into an integer before returning. A common pitfall is trusting the input will always be valid; readInt assumes digits are provided or performs simple parsing — your program should consider input validation. Takeaway: prefer these helpers when you need a complete user response instead of manual low‑level reads. readLine and readInt: Prompts and Parsing means readline collects characters into a dynamic string until enter; readint reads characters and parses them into an integer value.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

In Jack, a string is represented as an object with a small fixed layout: a length field for the current number of characters, a maxLength that records the allocated capacity, and a charArray pointer that references the dynamically allocated character buffer. The buffer itself is allocated using Memory. alloc. Because the string object contains references and a pointer to additional heap storage, it must be constructed at runtime using String. new and later disposed if no longer needed. This differs from static arrays because each string can have a different maxLength and can be resized by creating a larger buffer and copying content if desired. A concrete example: calling String. new(64) would allocate space for the String object and call Memory. alloc(64) to reserve a charArray of 64 characters. The length starts at zero. appendChar increments length and writes into the next slot; eraseLastChar decrements length. A common misconception is assuming strings are fixed or implicitly garbage collected; in Jack they are explicit objects managed by the programmer. Takeaway: think of a string as a small header plus a separately allocated character buffer managed through Memory. alloc and explicit lifecycle calls.

The String module exposes operations that manipulate the header and the charArray. appendChar checks that the current length is less than maxLength, writes the new character into charArray[length], and increments length. charAt returns charArray[i] after bounds checking. setCharAt writes to the given index if within bounds. eraseLastChar decrements length and may optionally clear the slot. These operations are simple but the implementation must carefully manage length and ensure not to write past maxLength. A concrete example: consider appending three characters to a newly created string new(4). After each append length increases 0→1→2→3 and the characters occupy indices 0,1,2. If you try to append a fifth character you should either return an error or ignore the append, depending on your design. A common misconception is assuming that appendChar will automatically grow the buffer; in Jack, buffer growth requires explicit allocation and copying. Takeaway: test edge cases: empty strings, full buffers, and invalid indices for charAt and setCharAt so your code fails predictably rather than corrupting memory. The chapter focuses on polling because the Hack platform provides a memory-mapped keyboard register and no kernel event queue. Polling repeatedly checks that register to detect key presses.
